newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - April 15.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - April 15.

text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

According to a confidential report by the Office of Government Information Technology, the federal government plans to cut up to A$824 million - nearly a third of its computer spending - over five years from information technology expenditure by overhauling government data centres and outsourcing the technical support and management of 130,000 desktop computers. Page 1.

A worldwide survey entitled Future Direction: The Power of the Competitive Board was released yesterday, throwing the competitiveness of Australia's company boards into question. Sponsored by the Australian Institute of Company Directors, the report found that as few as 20 to 25 percent of directors surveyed monitored results outside formal board meetings. Page 3.

The National Competition Council is set to conduct a comprehensive review of Australia Post's monopoly status, with industry sources saying the crucial issue will be whether new entrants to the postal market could get effective access to Australia Post's delivery network. Federal Treasurer Peter Costello is said to have recently asked his state counterparts for their input into the review's terms of reference. Page 3.

According to a Morgan poll published in this week's Bulletin, 85 percent of the public believe Independent Senator Mal Colston should resign from Parliament. The poll was carried out on April 9-10 when Prime Minister John Howard withdrew support from the embattled senator. Results from the poll, which surveyed 554 people, went on to reveal that 81 percent believe the rorts affair has damaged public trust in Parliament. Page 5.
THE AUSTRALIAN

In a move reflecting government frustration that after three months of talks, Aborigines, miners, pastoralists and the states have not been able to reach an agreement on a response to the High Court's controversial Wik ruling, Prime Minister John Howard will intensify pressure on Aborigines to accept a compromise on the politically sensitive issue by telling Cabinet today he will consider extinguishing native title over pastoral leases if the parties do not accept his native title blueprint. Page 1.

While senior federal government ministers played down the chances of a dispute with Iran resulting in trade sanctions, the Coalition faced renewed pressure from the United States, some backbenchers, and Jewish lobbyists to abandon a A$1 billion line of credit with Iran as Foreign Affairs Minister Alexander Downer prepares to brief Cabinet today on Australia's position regarding the diplomatic row with Tehran over its alleged sponsorship of international terrorism. Page 1.

Amid widespread confusion and anxiety among tens of thousands of Hong Kong-born Australians about their rights in the territory following the end of British colonial rule in July, the federal government plans to warn Hong Kong migrants they could lose their rights as Australian citizens as the territory assumes Chinese rule. Page 1.

Opening the 12th South Pacific Judicial Conference in Sydney yesterday, Australian Chief Justice Sir Gerard Brennan supported a call by the eight Chief Justices of the states and territories for greater judicial independence and reminded politicians that while they come and go, courts had to remain impartial. Page 3.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

In a move which will put Aboriginal leaders under intense pressure to give more ground in discussions on the High Court's controversial Wik ruling and is aimed at placating senior Queensland National Party members who have threatened to quit the Coalition, Prime Minister John Howard has announced he is willing to extinguish native title on pastoral leases if there was no agreement with farmers. Page 1.

Under new rules announced by China yesterday, which have been cautiously welcomed by leaders of Australia's Chinese community, the 100,000 Hong Kong residents who have moved to other countries - including up to 30,000 who have moved to Australia - will have 18 months to return to Hong Kong after the July 1 handover to Chinese rule if they wish to retain their permanent residency status in the territory. Page 1.

In a move which consumer groups fear will soon be followed by other banks after the release of the Wallis inquiry into the financial system, Colonial State Bank has doubled its fees on its everyday deposit and savings accounts and will levy a charge for all EFTPOS purchases. Page 1.

Brian Powers, the managing director of Kerry Packer's Consolidated Press Holdings, has threatened to sue the ABC over a Four Corners report dealing with management of the Sydney Harbour Casino and the sale of a waste-to-energy business to Australian National Industries which he claims is "highly defamatory". Page 1.
THE AGE

On the eve of a Federal Cabinet meeting in Brisbane, senior Queensland National Party members last night warned of a possible split in the Coalition unless Prime Minister John Howard extinguishes native title rights on pastoral leases. The move comes amid fears Howard will seek codification of the rights of pastoralists and Aborigines in legislation. Page A1.

In Victoria's sixth food outbreak in a month, about 30 people have fallen ill, with at least five admitted to hospital with symptoms of dehydration and gastroenteritis, after eating chicken curry at an Indonesian food festival at Malvern at the weekend. According to health authorities, the outbreak appears to be linked to poor food handling. Page A1.

Senate President Margaret Reid's attempt yesterday to ask embattled Senator Mal Colston to resign from the deputy presidency amid controversy over his alleged travel rorts was foiled when she was told by the Wesley Hospital that Colston would not be taking calls. Page A1.

A study by the Australian Institute of Family Studies of people married for 30 years or more indicates marital bliss has a lot to do with the way couples argue, with 60 percent of couples saying calmly discussing disagreements works for them. The study found 97 percent of respondents considered their marriage to be happy. Page A1.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
